title: The Galah Survey: Classification and Diagnostics with t‑SNE Reduction of Spectral Information
abstract: Abstract Galah is an ongoing high‑resolution spectroscopic survey with the goal of disentangling the formation history of the Milky Way using the fossil remnants of disrupted satellite galaxies. It is targeting a randomly selected magnitude‑limited sample of stars, aiming for one million spectra. So far more than 300 000 spectra have been obtained. Not all spectra are well‑behaved for parameter pipelines, and so a tool is needed to flag peculiar objects. We present a semi‑automated classification scheme for identifying peculiar spectra, based on t‑distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t‑SNE). The method maps the high‑dimensional spectral data into a 2‑D plane, preserving local similarity. We find that the majority of the 209 533 Galah spectra in our sample correspond to normal stars, but 31 053 show peculiar spectral signatures. Among these we identify cool metal‑poor giants, binaries, emission‑line objects, Hα‑emitting stars, and Li‑rich stars. The catalog of peculiar objects is provided, together with follow‑up priorities.

title: ROOSTER: a machine‑learning analysis tool for Kepler stellar rotation periods
abstract: In order to understand stellar evolution, it is crucial to efficiently determine stellar surface rotation periods. Indeed, while they are of great importance in stellar models, angular momentum transport processes inside stars are still poorly understood today. Surface rotation, which is linked to the age of the star, is one of the constraints needed to improve the way those processes are modelled. Statistics of the surface rotation periods for a large sample of stars of different spectral types are thus necessary. An efficient tool to automatically determine reliable rotation periods is needed when dealing with large samples of stellar photometric datasets. The objective of this work is to develop such a tool. For this purpose, machine learning classifiers constitute relevant bases to build our new methodology. Random forest learning abilities are exploited to automate the extraction of rotation periods in Kepler light curves. Rotation periods and complementary parameters are obtained via three different methods: a wavelet analysis, the autocorrelation function of the light curve, and the composite spectrum. We trained three different classifiers: one to detect if rotational modulations are present in the light curve, one to flag close binary or classical pulsators candidates that can bias our rotation period determination, and finally one classifier to provide the final rotation period. We tested our machine learning pipeline on 23 431 stars of the Kepler K and M dwarf reference rotation catalogue for which 60% of the stars have been visually inspected. For the sample of 21 707 stars where all the input parameters are provided to the algorithm, 94.2% of them are correctly classified (as rotating or not). Among the stars that have a rotation period in the reference catalogue, the machine learning provides a period that agrees within 10% of the reference value for 95.3% of the stars. Moreover, the yield of correct rotation periods is raised to 99.5% after visually inspecting 25.2% of the stars. Over the two main analysis steps, rotation classification and period selection, the pipeline yields a global agreement with the reference values of 92.1% and 96.9% before and after visual inspection. Random forest classifiers are efficient tools to determine reliable rotation periods in large samples of stars. The methodology presented here could be easily adapted to extract surface rotation periods for stars with different spectral types or observed by other instruments such as K2, TESS or by PLATO in the near future.

title: Experimental Analysis of Stellar Classification by using Different Machine Learning Algorithms
abstract: In advanced Astrophysics, Machine Learning has progressively attained popularity with its astounding powerful potential to analyze large amounts of data and make accurate predictions. The categorization of stars is based on their spectral features, known as stellar classification. The star's electromagnetic energy is studied by dividing it using a diffraction or prism grating into a spectrum that has a rainbow of colours intermingled with spectral lines that are used for classification. The use of space‑based imaging surveys necessitates a considerable deal of information on the spectral types of stars. This research presents the techniques for classifying stellar features into a Galaxy and a Star using various Machine Learning Algorithms on a dataset consisting of 100,000 observations. Techniques like K‑Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), and Naïve Bayes (NB) are used to train the model. Ultimately, a relative examination is done based on investigational outcomes from distinct models. This experiment demonstrates that the Support Vector Classifier (SVC) provides the highest accuracy, whereas the Decision tree (DT) provides the lowest. Finally, the potential for additional research in this area is highlighted.

title: Dissecting stellar chemical abundance space with t‑SNE
abstract: In the era of large‑scale Galactic astronomy and multi‑object spectroscopic stellar surveys, the sample sizes and the number of available stellar chemical abundances have reached dimensions in which it has become difficult to process all the available information in an effective manner. In this paper we demonstrate the use of a dimensionality‑reduction technique (t‑distributed stochastic neighbour embedding; t‑SNE) for analysing the stellar abundance‑space distribution. While the non‑parametric non‑linear behaviour of this technique makes it difficult to estimate the significance of any abundance‑space substructure found, we show that our results depend little on parameter choices and are robust to abundance errors. By reanalysing the high‑resolution high‑signal‑to‑noise solar‑neighbourhood HARPS‑GTO sample with t‑SNE, we find clearer chemical separations of the high‑ and low‑[α/Fe] disc sequences, hints for multiple populations in the high‑[α/Fe] population, and indications that the chemical evolution of the high‑[α/Fe] metal‑rich stars is different from the rest of the high‑α disc.

title: Estimation of stellar atmospheric parameters from SDSS/SEGUE spectra
abstract: We present a method for estimating stellar atmospheric parameters (effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity) from low‑resolution SDSS/SEGUE stellar spectra using a machine‑learning algorithm, the kernel‑based support vector regression (SVR). We train the SVR on a set of 1600 real spectra of stars with known atmospheric parameters from the SEGUE Stellar Parameter Pipeline (SSPP). We test our method on 800 spectra not used in training. The SVR estimates Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] with typical uncertainties of 85 K, 0.18 dex, and 0.13 dex, respectively. These precisions are comparable to those achieved by the SSPP, but our method is much faster, taking only a fraction of a second per spectrum. Our approach provides an efficient alternative for estimating stellar atmospheric parameters for large spectroscopic surveys.

title: Asteroseismology of solar‑type stars
abstract: The field of asteroseismology, the study of stellar oscillations, has made spectacular progress in the past decade thanks to space missions such as CoRoT and Kepler. These missions have provided high‑quality photometric time series for hundreds of thousands of stars, allowing us to probe the interiors of stars. In this review we discuss the basic principles of asteroseismology and present some of the main results obtained for solar‑type stars. We focus on how asteroseismic data can constrain stellar masses, radii, ages, and internal structure. We also discuss the challenges and prospects for future space missions such as TESS and PLATO.

landing_page_url: Astrophysically robust systematics removal using variational inference: application to the first month of Kepler data
publication_year: Systematic effects present in astronomical time‑series data can severely hamper the scientific return of space‑based photometric missions. In this work, we present a fully probabilistic approach based on variational inference to remove instrumental systematics from stellar light curves. The method models both astrophysical signals and instrumental noise simultaneously within a Bayesian framework, and it does not require external calibration or prior knowledge of instrumental behaviour. We apply our algorithm to the first month of Kepler data and demonstrate that it efficiently removes systematics while preserving real astrophysical variability. The approach is fast and scalable to large datasets, making it suitable for future large‑scale photometric surveys.
label: 10.1093/mnras/stx662

landing_page_url: deep‑REMAP: Parameterization of Stellar Spectra Using Regularized Multi‑Task Learning
publication_year: Spectroscopic surveys generate huge volumes of stellar spectra, requiring efficient methods to derive stellar parameters. We present deep‑REMAP, a regularized multi‑task deep learning model to directly predict multiple stellar atmospheric parameters from observed spectra. The model is trained end‑to‑end on observed spectra, jointly predicting effective temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, and alpha abundance. Regularization is used to improve generalization performance, but the model’s core objective is parameter estimation, not spectral pre‑processing. We validate on real spectroscopic datasets and show competitive accuracy compared with traditional pipelines.

landing_page_url: Identification of Mine Mixed Water Inrush Source Based on Genetic Algorithm and XGBoost Algorithm: A Case Study of Huangyuchuan Mine
publication_year: Water inrush is one of the major hazards threatening safe mining operations. Rapid and accurate identification of water inrush sources is critical for disaster prevention and mitigation. In this paper, we propose an identification model for mine mixed water inrush sources combining genetic algorithm and XGBoost. The spectral data used are mine water quality spectra, unrelated to astronomical stellar observations. Experiments show that the hybrid GA‑XGBoost model achieves high classification accuracy for mine water source discrimination, providing a reference for mine water hazard early‑warning.
